videos.script: A pivot table tells you the numbers. A chart tells you what they mean, if it is the right chart. {{question}} So this lesson starts with the question, not the chart. Comparing products is bars. Change over months is a line. A share of a whole is sometimes a pie, and usually a bar again. {{pie}} Here are Café Serra's six products as a pie. Which slice is bigger? You cannot tell. As sorted bars, you can, and you can see by how little. {{bars}} Then you build them. One chart from a small summary of the months, and one PivotChart that follows the pivot table and its slicers. {{build}} Then the parts that make a chart honest. A title that says the finding. Axes with units. Bars that start at zero. {{axes}} Then the combo chart, and its trap. Put bags on a second axis, and you choose where the line sits. Set it one way, and bags follow revenue. Set it another, and bags never move. {{combo}} And last, sparklines. A tiny chart inside one cell, one per product, for the shape of eighteen months at a glance. {{sparklines}}
